transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-12
Start time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Carlos Mendes (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Anita Rao (Mistral Head Infra), Samir Patel (ML Infra Eng), Olivia Chen (SRE)

Summary (auto): quick alignment on recent tail spikes, dug into KV cache heatmaps and network asymmetry, looked at streaming tokenization artifacts; agreed on bench runs and follow-ups.

Transcript:
[00:00:06] Carlos (Redwood): okay hey everyone, thanks for joining — we wanted to dig in on the p95/p99 spikes you flagged last week. quick context: priya and i looked at the top-level traces, we see two recurring patterns — hot-shard evictions in the KV cache and a set of requests that go multi-hop across a peered region.
[00:00:36] Anita (Mistral): yep that's right, we've been seeing occasional 3-4x jumps at p99, usually coinciding with larger batch windows but not always. sometimes during low qps too which is weird.
[00:00:52] Priya (Redwood SE): one possibility is asymmetric network paths — packets take a longer route to the kv store node in one AZ, then fallback to a cold cache path. that increases serialization time for the kv lookup.
[00:01:18] Samir (Mistral): we did a quick traceroute and saw some inconsistent hop counts between AZ-east-1a and 1c, but that was adhoc. i'll run a more thorough matrix.
[00:01:33] Olivia (Mistral SRE): also we saw that during some bursts, a single worker gets hammered by very similar prefixes which creates a hot-key pattern in our prefix-KV layer — we're calling them 'hot-shards'.
[00:01:50] Carlos: cool, those two hypotheses are what we prepared for. priya, do you want to walk through the KV eviction trace we pulled?
[00:02:02] Priya: sure — so on the trace, eviction events line up with token windowing on longer contexts. the runtime tries to keep kv for the active prefix, but when the same prefix arrives at high concurrency, the per-shard LRU gets churned. eviction causes a read to backing store or to a remote shard which adds 30-120 ms on top of generation latency. note: in some transcriptions the tool labeled these as 'KV cash' — it's kv cache.
[00:02:41] Samir: is that read to backing store always over the network? or can it be local disk on the same host?
[00:02:50] Priya: depends on topology. we saw examples of both: local disk (slower than memory but okay) and remote shard reads (which are the worst). when remote, you get the added network hop — sometimes through a NAT gateway which doubles the path.
[00:03:08] Anita: we run mixed instances; some are on-prem racks peered via VPN into our VPC, so there are asymmetric paths by design. that's probably amplifying it.
[00:03:21] Carlos: that aligns. one quick thing — MTU mismatches on tunnels can cause fragment and reassembly overhead, which shows up as extra latency under load. it's low probability but high impact.
[00:03:38] Olivia: good point, we had an MTU problem last year, forgot about it. we'll check.
[00:03:45] [00:03:45] Priya: next, streaming vs non-streaming — we instrumented both. streaming reduces perceived latency for the client but increases number of interrupts for the serving process. in our tests, streaming with small token churn increased p99 by ~15% on the hottest endpoints because scheduling interrupts prevented timely batching.
[00:04:10] Samir: interesting. so streaming may help avg latency or tail for small outputs, but for multi-token streams it hurts because you can't batch effectively?
[00:04:22] Priya: exactly. if the workload is lots of < 8-token responses, streaming helps. if many responses are 50-200 tokens, you want to let the runtime coalesce tokens into larger batch windows.
[00:04:36] Anita: our product needs both; chat UI uses streaming, but some analytics pipelines use large non-streaming responses. how do we handle that mix?
[00:04:48] Carlos: common pattern is adaptive mode: use streaming by default for interactive sessions and enable a batching override for known high-throughput flows. also, set different routing policies so streaming sessions hit nodes with higher preemption budgets.
[00:05:02] Priya: another lever is prefix/KV co-location — pin hot prefixes to a subset of nodes so their KV lookups are local and avoid remote hops. but that has operational cost.
[00:05:15] Samir: we saw entries where the prefix pinning was not honored after autoscaler scaled down — eviction/reshard logic moved keys.
[00:05:25] Priya: yes, autoscaler churn is a tricky part. we recommend a warm pool and controlled shrink to keep pinned shards stable. also, reinforcing TTLs and prefetch heuristics helps.
[00:05:36] Olivia: about quantization — some of our teams pushed 4-bit quant for cost but noticed higher variance in runtime. is quantization adding to the tail?
[00:05:48] Carlos: quant introduces two things: lower compute time per token on average but increases kernel branching if not using contiguous memory formats. on some GPUs, lower-bit kernels are less mature and jitter more. also, dequant/req paths can create extra CPU/GPU sync points.
[00:06:06] Priya: in our benchmarks, 4-bit q8 with the right kernel gave 20% cost savings and similar p50, but p99 could be worse if the kernel falls back to a safe but slower implementation under certain sequence lengths. we log a kernel-fallback metric in the runtime.
[00:06:27] Samir: is that something you can flag in logs? we want to correlate p99 events to kernel fallback traces.
[00:06:33] Priya: yes we can add a tag per invocation: kernel_variant=fast|fallback, and add that to your perf traces. we'll include it in the next perf run.
[00:06:42] Anita: networking — you said NAT double-hop earlier. how common is that in cloud peering?
[00:06:49] Carlos: surprisingly common when customers use VPNs and transit gateways; if a request from compute in us-east hits a NAT in us-east, then peered transit in us-west, you get path asymmetry. traceroutes and flow logs reveal it. also watch for AWS ENI limits causing cross-host forwarding.
[00:07:07] Olivia: should we expect 30-100ms penalties from those detours?
[00:07:12] Priya: in bad cases yes, especially if packets cross public internet or traverse older appliance hops. inside modern cloud regions it's usually < 5-15ms, but the added jitter pushes p99.
[00:07:25] [00:07:25] Samir: okay let's talk instrumentation. what do you need from us to correlate p99?
[00:07:31] Carlos: ideal set: per-request trace id, kernel_variant, kv-shard-id, kv-eviction-flag, routing-path-id, and whether streaming used. that lets us slice p99 by each dimension.
[00:07:47] Anita: we can add those fields to our logs. Samir, can you scope the instrumentation work?
[00:07:53] Samir: yes, i can add them. may take a day to wire into prod logs.
[00:07:58] Priya: on batching tuning — we noticed that under low qps, aggressive batching windowing increases latency; under high qps it reduces cost. so the runtime uses a dynamic window that adapts to observed qps and tail slope. we recommended a floor and ceiling for the window to avoid extremes.
[00:08:20] Olivia: what's the recommended floor/ceiling?
[00:08:23] Priya: default is 10ms floor, 50ms ceiling for interactive workloads; for analytics you can bump floor to 30ms to get larger batches. but if network hops add >20ms those windows need reconsideration.
[00:08:37] Carlos: also enable prefix-aware batching so tokens from the same session are prioritized together. without that, session interleaving can blow up tail.
[00:08:46] [00:08:46] Anita: can we run a focused bench that injects asymmetric delay and hot-shard traffic to reproduce p99?
[00:08:53] Carlos: yes, that's exactly what we'll do. we'll provide a test harness (kv-hottrace) that simulates hot prefixes, mixes streaming/non-streaming, and can optionally inject delay on certain paths.
[00:09:06] Priya: test plan: 1) reproduce baseline, 2) inject 15-50ms delay on half the kv shard lookups, 3) toggle streaming vs non-streaming, 4) run quantization profiles 4-bit/8-bit/float16.
[00:09:21] Samir: timeline?
[00:09:23] Carlos: we'll aim to run step 1-3 in staging by 11/18, quant runs the following week.
[00:09:29] [00:09:29] Priya: quick note on observability — add p99-by-prefix dashboards and kernel-fallback counters. that'll make trend alerts meaningful.
[00:09:40] Olivia: got it.
[00:09:44] Anita: one more product constraint — we need persisted audit logs for a compliance audit; adding too many per-request tags increases storage costs. can we sample?
[00:09:54] Carlos: yes sample at 1% for full traces and 100% for kernel_fallback events; that'll give high-fidelity for anomalies without exploding budget.
[00:10:04] Priya: also, for hot-key detection you can compute an online heatmap with sketches rather than full traces — much cheaper.
[00:10:13] Samir: good.
[00:10:16] [00:10:16] Anita: are there any quick wins we can do in config before the bench runs?
[00:10:21] Priya: enable prefetch for known hot prefixes, increase warm pool size to reduce reshards on scale-down, and set streaming token aggregation for sessions longer than 12 tokens.
[00:10:34] Carlos: and check MTU on your VPN and peering tunnels. that's a quick infrastructure ticket.
[00:10:40] Olivia: i'll create the MTU ticket now after this call.
[00:10:44] [00:10:44] Samir: a weird observation — sometimes p99 correlates to gc pauses in the host JVM that runs a small shim. could that be a factor?
[00:10:53] Priya: yes if there's a JVM or Python process doing serialization/pre/post-processing, a stop-the-world pause can cause a tail event. instrument host-level metrics (cpu steal, gc) alongside request traces.
[00:11:07] Carlos: we also noticed kernel placements matter — GPU host oversubscription can move some latency into the p99. ensure your scheduler avoids packing high-latency kernels together.
[00:11:18] Anita: any recommended node sizing for mixed streaming + batch workloads?
[00:11:22] Priya: pick nodes with slightly higher mem-to-gpu ratio to keep KV in memory and allow larger prefetch. for streaming workloads prefer lower core count but higher NIC throughput to minimize interrupts.
[00:11:36] Carlos: we have a doc with tuned profiles; i'll send it after the call — it includes best-practice kernel flags, quant matrices, and batching floors.
[00:11:44] Anita: great.
[00:11:46] [00:11:46] Priya: questions from the Mistral team?
[00:11:49] Samir: when you run the kv-hottrace harness, will it produce per-request kernel_variant and route_id out of the box?
[00:11:55] Priya: yes. it dumps traces to s3 and attaches a perf.csv with the dimensions we discussed. we'll include a sample dashboard.
[00:12:03] Olivia: do you have a recommended sampling rate for full traces vs perf counters?
[00:12:09] Priya: 1% full traces, 100% lightweight counters and kernel_fallback markers.
[00:12:15] [00:12:15] Carlos: last note on fallback policies — runtime can fall back from a quantized kernel to a safe kernel when an edge-case sequence length occurs. that fallback is expensive and often invisible without kernel_variant tagging. it's a major driver of p99.
[00:12:34] Anita: ok, so tagging & sampling is highest priority then bench harness.
[00:12:40] Carlos: yes. we'll also include a small checklist for infra — MTU, traceroutes, ENI limits, NAT paths.
[00:12:48] [00:12:48] Priya: i'll attach the kernel_variant docs and a sample perf dashboard link in the follow-up.
[00:12:55] Carlos: cool. shall we recap next steps?
[00:13:00] Anita: go ahead.
[00:13:02] Carlos: recap: Carlos will send the perf templates, quant matrices, and tuned runtime flags by 11/16. Priya will run the kv-hottrace in staging and share results by 11/18. Mistral (Anita/Samir/Olivia) will run MTU/traceroutes and wire the proposed instrumentation into logs by 11/15. we'll sync after the bench completes — propose 11/20 for a follow up readout.
[00:13:26] Samir: sounds good.
[00:13:28] Olivia: yes.
[00:13:30] Anita: thanks everyone.
[00:13:33] Carlos: thanks, talk soon.

[00:13:36] End of recorded portion — the team stayed for a short private sync about pricing and plan options (not recorded here).

Notes about transcript quality: automatic transcription had occasional speaker swap (Priya labeled as 'Speaker 2' on a few segments) and some mis-hearings ("KV cash" for KV cache). We preserved filler words and interruptions to keep authenticity.
